Seedy

SEE-dee -- originally 'full of seeds,' from a plant that has 'gone to seed' and looks worn out; by the 1800s the word had come to mean shabby or disreputable. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Seedy is sleazy, shabby, and disreputable.

The detective's office was in a seedy part of downtown, above a pawnshop with bars on the windows.

Worked Example

A traveler checks into a motel with a flickering neon sign, stained carpets, and a lock that barely latches.

That shabby, slightly disreputable atmosphere is exactly what seedy describes -- run-down enough to feel a little unsafe or untrustworthy.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disreputable: A disreputable place or person has earned a bad name -- people have heard things and steer clear. Seedy is about what you can see: the peeling paint, the stained carpet, the run-down look that makes a place feel untrustworthy before you know anything about it.

shady: A shady business or character makes you suspect dishonest dealings -- money changes hands off the books, and questions get dodged. Seedy points at appearance instead of behavior: a seedy motel may be perfectly honest, just run-down enough to make its guests uneasy.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

immaculate: spotlessly clean and neat

reputable: having a good, trustworthy reputation

Where it sits · how visibly run-down it looks — shabby → seedy → squalid

shabby vs. seedy: Shabby is milder than seedy -- a shabby coat or armchair is merely worn and faded, while seedy adds an unsavory, slightly unsafe air on top of the shabbiness.

squalid vs. seedy: Squalid is stronger and more extreme than seedy -- squalid conditions are filthy and often linked to real poverty or neglect, while seedy just means shabby and a bit disreputable.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — seed-

root — seed-: from a plant gone to seed, worn out (Old English (saed))

suffix — -y

suffix — -y: characterized by, full of (Old English)

Put it together

Put it together: Seedy literally meant 'full of seeds' -- describing a plant that has gone to seed and started to look ragged and worn out -- and by the nineteenth century the word had shifted to describe run-down, disreputable places and people in that same worn-out way.

Use the root in a new word: seedling

Use the root in a new word: seedling: The greenhouse sold tomato seedlings every spring for home gardeners.

Root Check

Word Choice

Seedy is a fairly informal word, usually describing a place, neighborhood, or business that looks run-down and makes people uneasy -- it's rarely used to describe a person's character directly, though 'seedy characters' is a common phrase for shady individuals.
